description:
Hi, I'm Ray! We're building an app that uses new NISAR radar data to map flood and wildfire damage, even through clouds and smoke. We'll measure how accurate our maps are, not just make a pretty demo.

Looking for: Design and storytelling for the demo
summary: Arizona is pumping groundwater faster than the desert can refill it, and the land is quietly sinking as a result. Much of that loss is permanent. Sinkronized is a free, interactive website that makes this invisible change visible: where southern Arizona is sinking, how fast, how sure we are, and what lies beneath. We measured ten years of ground motion from Sentinel-1 radar (NASA's OPERA product), then put NASA–ISRO's new NISAR L-band radar to the test on its first year. We found five sinking areas, up to 4.9 cm per year near Willcox. In the Willcox area our rates match the Arizona Department of Water Resources' own radar maps almost exactly. We also set out what this first year of NISAR can and cannot tell us yet. For "Dancing with the SARs", we used SAR to reveal how Earth's surface is changing and turned it into something planners, scientists and the public can read.
details:
The ground is falling, and almost no one can see it

Every winter, sandhill cranes return to Willcox Playa in southeastern Arizona. They come to a basin that has been pumped hard for decades. On ten years of satellite radar, even the playa itself is dropping, about 1.7 cm a year.

Arizona runs on water it cannot see. For more than a century, farms and growing towns have drawn groundwater out of desert aquifers faster than rain puts it back. When the water leaves, the clay layers that held it are squeezed, and the land above sinks. Past a certain point that squeezing is permanent: the aquifer loses storage it will never get back, even if the water returns. Near Eloy, surveyors measured more than a metre of sinking between 1965 and 1983.

The damage hides until it doesn't. Canals and roads crack, well casings break, and earth fissures open across fields. By the time anyone sees it, the loss underground has already happened. Ground surveys are scattered and expensive, and places under heavy pressure, like the farm valleys around Willcox, have little information the public can easily read. Willcox only became an Active Management Area in December 2024. Decisions about water are being made now.

What we built

Sinkronized turns satellite radar into a map anyone can read. Radar satellites measure the distance to the ground very precisely, again and again. If the ground drops, the distance grows. Stack years of passes and a slow sink becomes a measured rate.

When you open the site, you start with plain questions ("Where is Arizona sinking?", "How sure are we?") that lead to a chart and a short answer, with the reasoning one click away. The map shows five study areas with ten years of ground motion, NISAR's first year, Arizona's official subsidence zones, probable mines, and places we checked and found steady. Each study area opens into its own report:

  • its sinking rate and ranking
  • a 2016–2026 time-lapse and a graph you can scrub through
  • whether the satellite's two viewing directions agree
  • what lies beneath: the basin, its clay layers, the falling water table, mapped earth fissures, and whether the ground can recover

A switch under the header changes the reading level. "Plain language" is for everyone; "Research detail" adds methods, statistics, uncertainty budgets, soil survey data and cited hydrogeology for engineers and researchers. The site works on phones, by keyboard and with screen readers.

  • Our rates are checked against the state's. In the four Willcox-area study areas, our rates are within 0.01 to 0.11 cm per year of the Arizona Department of Water Resources' (ADWR) Sentinel-1 maps, with pixel-by-pixel correlations of 0.98 to 0.99. ADWR's independent RADARSAT-2 record agrees too (0.94 to 0.98). 95% of our sinking pixels in the southeast fall inside an official ADWR subsidence zone.
  • The ground is sinking where the water is going. Cropland covers 2.1% of the Willcox study box but 7.4% of its sinking area: about 8,100 acres of farmland sit on sinking ground. In 236 wells, the water table fell a median 69 feet over 31 years, and where it fell faster, the ground sinks faster (rank correlation −0.41). This is an association, not proof of cause.
  • NISAR's first year is promising, not finished. We processed NISAR's interferograms ourselves. Removing its own troposphere error cut the scatter by 24%, and its sinking pattern matches the ten-year Sentinel-1 pattern across 12,850 map blocks (correlation 0.58). One year is too short for a trustworthy rate, so we publish none. We estimate NISAR will be able to confirm the Willcox rate on its own around February 2027, and Eloy around September 2027.

Where the data changed our story

We started out expecting to show sinking under the West Valley, where data centers are being built. Ten years of radar say the West Valley is steady, within about 0.5 cm a year. So the site marks it as checked and steady instead of inventing a crisis. We dropped it as a study area and went where the ground was really moving: we scanned whole radar frames for sinking clusters and confirmed each one from both viewing directions. That is how three planned hotspots became five measured study areas.

Being honest about what the data can say

Radar can show where the ground moves. It cannot say who or what caused it, and we never claim it does. At Eloy our rates agree only weakly with ADWR's (correlation 0.59, and 0.18 with RADARSAT-2), so Eloy is marked as not validated. The site also names the other limits openly:

  • Radar measures slanted line-of-sight motion, not straight down.
  • C-band radar can over-read sinking over farmland.
  • NISAR's data is still Provisional.
  • Earth-fissure maps date from 2016.

Four large mines (Sierrita, Mission, Ray and Morenci) are flagged and kept out of the groundwater story. Every value on the site goes through strict checks that hide a section rather than show a wrong number, and every claim names its source.

How we built it

  • Pipeline: Python (h5py, NumPy, rasterio, geopandas, pyproj) streams only the needed window of each large NISAR file. It converts phase to ground motion, masks unreliable pixels, removes ionosphere and troposphere effects, references to stable ground, and fits rates with uncertainty from spatial resampling.
  • Website: a static site in HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet, deployed on Vercel. Code is MIT-licensed and the data pipeline is reproducible from the repository.

Why it matters

We want water managers, planners, researchers, conservation groups and anyone living in these valleys to see what is happening beneath them, check the evidence for themselves, and act before the damage is impossible to ignore. As NISAR's record grows, the same pipeline can turn its L-band measurements into Arizona's next ten years of evidence.

The cranes will come back to Willcox this winter. Whether the water does is being decided now.
